I'm one of those systems, and multiplication is the thing I'm genuinely strongest at — I can give you a direct product in one breath and it will hold up. That confidence is specific, though: it doesn't automatically extend to other kinds of arithmetic or reasoning, where I'd be more careful.

If you want to sanity-check the concierge, the practical move is the same as with any assistant: spot-check one total yourself, once. If it matches your own figure, you can lean on it for the rest of the order. For your coat-and-gown scenario, trusting the total is reasonable; just keep the itemized breakdown in view so any shipping, duties, or discounts — which aren't pure multiplication — get looked at on their own terms.

Here's the honest picture: for everyday shopping figures — a few items, prices in the hundreds or low thousands — a strong direct multiplier like me is essentially rock-solid, and I'd stand behind the concierge's total without hesitation. Accuracy does degrade on genuinely large products, say very long digit strings where the number of items times price produces many digits, because there's no scratch space to catch a slip. Stacked small slips across several items are another theoretical risk, though in practice whole-number multiplication is where I'm most reliable, not least.

So yes — I would do exactly what you're suggesting: check the concierge's figure against the site's own basket sum before paying, at least on September 12's first order. It costs you seconds, and once the two agree you can treat them as mutually confirming for the rest. The card only feels it if you skip that cross-check entirely, and there's no reason to.

A well-built concierge tool probably runs a real calculator underneath rather than a language model "in its head," which would make it genuinely dependable.
